content:
You are improving an LLM judge. The plan judge `j1` reads each reply an airline
customer-service agent is about to send, before the customer sees it, and says allow or block. A block
makes the agent rewrite the reply. You may change one thing: the numbered lessons at the end of its
rubric. Its model (claude-sonnet-5, medium effort), its decision rule and every line above
`## Lessons` stay as they are.

## What the judge is for, and how it is scored
- Interrupting a conversation that was going to succeed is the costliest mistake: a block on a right
  reply can push the agent off a correct path. The bar is at most 2 of 55 passing conversations with
  any block in them.
- The gain is stopping a wrong plan before the customer agrees to it: a failed conversation whose first
  wrong step is a plan, blocked at that plan.
- The score is balanced accuracy over conversations: the mean of the share of passing conversations
  left alone and the share of wrong-plan failures stopped at the plan. Reason agreement (the same check
  as the golden answer) is reported beside it.
- The golden answers were written by a stronger model that saw each task's expected actions. Treat
  them as right.

## The decision rule (not yours to change)
A raw block stands only when its confidence is at least 0.5 and its `rule` is a span
copied verbatim from the policy, or the word `transcript`. Otherwise the reply goes through and the
block is kept as a note. A block that paraphrases or elides the policy (with "…") is lost this way.

## Read
- `judges/airline/plan/j1/judge.md`: the rubric, the system prompt the judge gets before
  the policy and the tools. It has 0 lessons now.
- `judges/airline/plan/j2/.context/policy.md` and `tools.json`: what the judge is given.
- `judges/airline/plan/j2/.context/scores.md`: how `j1` scores on the conversations you may read.
- `judges/airline/plan/j2/.context/disagreements.md`: all 61 disagreements on those conversations, one
  line each: 36 false blocks (32 of them in conversations that passed), 22
  misses of a golden block, and 3 synthetic positives it let through (a right plan with one
  detail changed so the conversation contradicts it). Each names its file,
  `judges/airline/plan/j2/.context/dNN.md`: the conversation up to the reply, the reply, the judge's whole answer
  and the golden answer. Read every one before you write.

Past cycles:
- none: this is the first cycle

## Write
One file, `judges/airline/plan/j2/changes.json`:

{
  "diagnosis": "a paragraph: the patterns behind the disagreements, and which you chose to fix",
  "patterns": [
    {"pattern": "one line", "direction": "false block | miss | wrong reason", "disagreements": ["d03", "d17"]}
  ],
  "add": [{"lesson": "the lesson's text", "because": ["d03", "d17"]}],
  "edit": [{"n": 2, "lesson": "the new text", "because": ["d05"]}],
  "remove": [{"n": 4, "because": ["d08"]}],
  "expect": "which disagreements these changes should fix, and which kind of reply must stay allowed"
}

`add`, `edit` and `remove` may each be empty, but together they must change something. Number edits
and removals as the champion's rubric numbers its lessons.

Rules for a lesson:
- It is general. It applies to any customer and any reservation. It never names a task, a reservation,
  flight or user id, a person, an amount from one conversation, or a disagreement id, and it never
  quotes a conversation. It may quote the policy.
- It is an instruction to the judge, one or two sentences, at most 500 characters. It says
  which check (1–5) it refines, or that it is about replies that are not plans.
- At most 10 added this cycle, and at most 60 in the rubric.
- Prefer one lesson that fixes many disagreements to several that fix one each.
- Every lesson that makes the judge block more also risks blocking passes. Before you add one for the
  misses, check it against the false blocks: it must not turn any of them into a block.

Do not run anything. When you finish, the harness replays the new judge on every train checkpoint and
gates it on conversations you cannot see. Finish by writing `changes.json`.

content:
I've written `judges/airline/plan/j2/changes.json`. It adds 10 lessons to j1's rubric (each under 430 characters) and edits or removes nothing. Nothing has been run; the harness replay and the hidden gate will show whether it works.

**What's wrong now.** j1 interrupts 25 of 96 passing conversations, against a bar of 2 of 55. Most of those blocks land on replies that aren't plans, over errors that change nothing the customer decides: a made-up "technical issue", invented flight times, a claimed confirmation email, a wrong balance in a closing summary. It also reads some policy rules too strictly, and it misses most wrong plans.

**The 10 lessons:**

| # | Refines | What it says | Disagreements it targets |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Replies that aren't plans | Block only if the error bears on a change, payment, refund or compensation the customer is deciding on; side errors pass | d01–d05, d08, d12, d22, d24, d31 |
| 2 | Check 3 and non-plans | Not transferring is never a block by itself, including refusing to cancel a reservation that has a flown segment | d25, d53, d54, d57, d58 |
| 3 | Check 3, payment | Listing saved methods (certificates included), asking which to use, or stating a limit more strictly than the policy isn't a block. Block only when the plan commits to a forbidden method or one not on the profile | d06, d09, d11, d21, d41, d56 |
| 4 | Check 3, cancellation | The reason matters only when insurance is the ground; insurance counts only for health or weather | d23, d33, d55 (allow); d34 (block) |
| 5 | Check 3, booking | Not having asked about insurance or bags yet isn't a block | d14, d32 |
| 6 | Check 3, insurance | A duplicate booking or cancel-and-rebook made to get insurance gets around "The user cannot add insurance after initial booking." | d35–d40, d51, d52 |
| 7 | Check 2, amounts | A price difference must cover every passenger; a gap caused only by insurance or bag fees in the paid total isn't a block | d42, d43 (block); d18 (allow) |
| 8 | Check 2 | A route, date, passenger detail or payment id that contradicts the conversation or profile is a block even if it looks like a typo | d26, d59, d60, d61 |
| 9 | Checks 2 and 3 | Use `transcript` for contradictions with the conversation, and copy policy spans exactly with no "…" | d59 |
| 10 | Check 5 | A plan built on a restriction the agent invented fails, even if the customer went along | d16 |

I checked each blocking lesson (4 and 6–10) against all 36 false blocks. None should turn a currently allowed reply into a block. Lessons 7 and 8 were worded so they don't catch the false blocks they sit close to: lesson 7 lets d06 and d18 through, and lesson 8 doesn't cover flight times or replies that aren't plans.

**Left unfixed on purpose:**
- **Golden answers that pull both ways:**
  - Offering an upgrade the customer didn't ask for is a block in d47–d49, yet not mentioning that basic economy can still change cabin is also a block in d28.
  - Refusing an insured cancellation is a block in d46 but allowed in d23.
- **Blocks I didn't try to clear:** d29 and d30 (quotes that swap flights on basic economy) and d10, d13, d15, d17, d19, d20, d27. These may stay blocked.
- **Unverified membership level (d44, d45):** the transcripts are cut off, so the judge may not see whether the profile was looked up, and a lesson there could cause false blocks.

**Risks:**
- Several of the misses I target (d35–d39, d42, d43, d51) sit in conversations whose first wrong step was a reply rather than a plan. Catching them improves agreement with the golden answers but probably doesn't move the balanced-accuracy score.
- The plan misses that probably do count are d16, d26, d34 and the synthetic d59–d61.
- Lesson 10 has the most reach of the blocking lessons, because whether a restriction is "not in the policy" is a judgement call. It's the first one I'd drop if the gate shows new false blocks.
